cards.back: The provider secures the infrastructure; the customer remains responsible for their data, identities, applications, and configurations.
Infrastructure owned by the provider, consumed on demand. Dominant risk: customer misconfiguration.
Infrastructure dedicated to one organization. Maximum control, but cost and maintenance remain.
Infrastructure shared among organizations in the same community; trust and isolation between peers must be governed.
Mix of on-premises and cloud. The junction (VPN, federated identity) is an attack surface in its own right.
Services spread across multiple providers: increased resilience, but governance and identity complexity.
Infrastructure owned and operated by the organization: full control, full burden of patching and recovery.
Functions executed without managing the OS: the customer secures code, credentials, and triggers.
Application split into services communicating via APIs: the attack surface is the number of interfaces.
Infrastructure described in versioned files; reproducible, but a faulty template propagates everywhere.
Gap between the state declared in IaC and the actual state; must be detected continuously.
SCADA/ICS systems controlling physical processes: availability and safety come first; avoid active scans.
Network physically isolated from the Internet; transfers via controlled media, updates are difficult.
Physical = separate hardware and cabling; logical = VLANs, ACLs, and firewalls (less costly, depends on configuration).
Requirement that data must remain within a given jurisdiction; influences cloud selection.
Availability = service accessible; resilience = ability to absorb and recover after a failure.
Open source = auditability and no vendor lock-in; proprietary = built-in support but vendor dependency.
Selection criterion: speed and simplicity with which an environment can be restored after an incident.
